A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same order-marginalized generative classification study. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original classifier training, ImageNet and WILDS evaluations, token-order experiments, tokenizer ablations and runtime measurements.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds RAR, masked-diffusion, ObjectNet/COCO and MeanFlow evaluations, among other analyses.

M1.justification: The central RandAR classifier and Equation (5) remain unchanged. Section 6.6 adds an adaptation of RAR trained without order annealing, and Section 6.7 introduces alternative masked-prefix scoring of RandAR. These extend the procedures without replacing the core method.

E1.justification: Appendix G adds ObjectNet and COCO evaluation while retaining the earlier ImageNet and WILDS coverage. These introduce non-image-centric object views and multi-object recognition, with COCO requiring recovery of multiple ImageNet-mapped objects rather than one class.

E2.justification: Table 6 adds comparisons involving adapted RAR-B, MaskGIT-B and RandAR scored as masked diffusion. The WILDS comparison adds raster-order RandAR at both model sizes. Appendix I additionally evaluates three MeanFlow classifier variants against DiT, substantially expanding the evaluated comparison methods.

E3.justification: New protocols include B-scale AR/MD comparisons with evaluation-budget sweeps through K=60, COCO-to-ImageNet mapping with K-recall@K, and three MeanFlow scoring strategies. The WILDS tokenizer statement changes from MaskGIT to LlamaGen with noise, matching the existing Appendix A; this correction does not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds architecture generalization through RAR, AR-versus-MD scoring sensitivity to computation, an XL no-noise ablation, raster-order controls on WILDS, and generation-quality versus classification analysis. Appendix I also tests whether few-step generation translates into efficient classification. These substantially extend v1's retained analyses.

E5.justification: Both versions retain three-seed averaging for the WILDS discriminative baselines. v2 introduces no additional repeated-run disclosures, confidence intervals, significance tests or uncertainty-reporting practices. The new evaluation-budget sweeps concern scoring procedures rather than uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Table 2 revises the relabelled A-VARC+ rows: ImageNet-Val scores change from 0.683 to 0.717 for L and 0.661 to 0.719 for XL; RandAR's main scores remain unchanged. Substantial new results cover RAR/MD, XL augmentation, WILDS raster controls, ObjectNet/COCO, generation FID and MeanFlow. Table 12 places RandAR above DiT but below DINOv2 on both added datasets.

T1.justification: Unlike v1, Appendix D derives a claimed equivalence between the order-averaged AR objective and a masked-diffusion ELBO using expectations over masked subsets. This is a substantive theoretical addition. As written, Equation (6) introduces a 1/N normalization inconsistent with the earlier full-sequence likelihood definition.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction contributions and conclusion retain the same central claims: order marginalization improves AR classification, surpasses diffusion classifiers with up to 25-fold faster inference, and competes with DINOv2. The additions provide supporting evidence without changing these headline claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations concerning generalization beyond RandAR and practical differences between equivalent-in-expectation scoring objectives. Appendix H hypothesizes that perceptual fidelity increasingly dominates FID at low values, while Appendix I distinguishes fast generation from fast classification. Existing error explanations and computational limitations remain.

D1.justification: v2 supplies sources for the MaskGIT-B checkpoint and COCO-to-ImageNet mapping, documents disabling RAR order annealing, and makes the WILDS tokenizer description consistent with Appendix A. The original core training schedules, hardware disclosure and code/model access information are retained.

R1.justification: v2 explicitly connects its objective to masked-diffusion research and extends the efficiency discussion to contemporary few-step diffusion methods. These relationships, supported by new any-order/diffusion and MeanFlow/distillation citations, substantially broaden the research positioning beyond v1's discussion. Existing cited works are retained.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the narrative sequence are retained. v2 inserts Sections 6.6–6.7 and several appendix sections, introduces AO-AR terminology, adds the HSE affiliation and corrects names such as ResNet-151 to ResNet-152. These are localized additions and edits rather than extensive rewriting.

P2.justification: v2 adds the paired B-scale/MD tables, ObjectNet/COCO and FID tables, and a MeanFlow runtime plot. Table 4 gains model-size groups and the WILDS table gains raster rows. These substantially expand the visual evidence; the earlier qualitative Figure 9 is retained as Figure 10. Page margins also increase throughout.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important gaps in support for generality and efficiency through another AR architecture, WILDS raster controls, multi-object/non-image-centric evaluation and MeanFlow comparisons. These strengthen the central argument while documenting DINOv2's remaining advantages, and the WILDS tokenizer correction improves consistency. Equation (6)'s normalization problem weakens the theoretical addition, but the broader empirical validation provides a substantial overall benefit.
